Reduces input lag the launcher controls: controller profiles use a tightened dead zone and a faster response curve so the same stick travel turns further, controller event handling does no locking, and idle overlay redraws are skipped

Removes Nagle and delayed-ACK delays on launcher connections, keeps connections pooled so handshakes are already done, prefetches DNS for launcher and Bedrock server addresses, and stops background polls while you play. Cannot change the distance to a game server or its own response time.

While a game is running, keeps the launcher out of the way: serves cached news and update data instead of polling, and steps further back automatically when the device gets hot, low on memory, or battery saver is on. It only reduces work the launcher itself does — it never changes Minecraft\'s own graphics or framerate.

Applies host-level performance changes to the game process through the preloader: a faster allocator, a real-time render thread, performance-core pinning and the panel\'s top refresh rate. Every item is listed below with what it actually did, and can be turned off on its own if your device does not like it. It never claims a frame rate.
Master switch is off. Turn it on to apply the optimizations below.
The preloader is not loaded, so the game-side optimizations cannot be applied. Enable a mod, or check that the preloader native library is present.
Changes apply on the next game launch.
Game hooks are resolved by RTTI name at runtime and fall back to "skipped" when a build does not expose a verified slot. They are off by default because a wrong hook can change how the game renders.
Routes the game process\'s allocations through mimalloc, which is faster under the small-object churn Minecraft generates.
Puts the render and game threads at real-time priority so a busy background task cannot stall a frame.
Pins the render thread to the device\'s fast cores when the chip has a big.LITTLE layout.
Asks the panel for its highest same-resolution refresh rate, so the game is not capped at the default. Never changes resolution.
Skips rendering entities behind the camera. Advanced: installs a game hook and falls back to skipped when the build has no verified slot.
Caps the number of particles drawn per frame. Advanced: installs a game hook and falls back to skipped when the build has no verified slot.
Steps the render distance down when the frame rate sits low for a sustained period, and back up when it recovers. Advanced: installs a game hook.
Watches the per-frame callback and reports its rate to the render-distance governor. Advanced: installs a game hook.
Watches the in-game HUD updates so the launcher can tell the HUD is live. Advanced: installs a game hook, off by default.

Off by default. Enable to run the closed-source gxcore verification stack. Leave off to skip it, which avoids a silent process exit right after "Loading native library: libgxcore.so" on devices where verification cannot complete

Capes, accessories and pets are drawn by the native cosmetics renderer, which the client hooks into the game\'s own player renderer. The preview shows your own skin wearing the equipped cape, accessory and pet, and pets animate their walk, run, crouch, fly and swim gaits here. All three reach the running game through that native hook as soon as they are equipped, with no resource pack and no world reload. Cosmetic sync shows them to other Glowberry users in the same world. Vanilla players do not see them — Bedrock gives an app no way to push a cosmetic onto someone else\'s account — and the pet is drawn on your own player rather than spawned as an entity, so it needs no server command and cannot trip a server check.

Each style is a real, different mesh — a cap, a beanie, a crown, horns, a halo and so on are separate geometry. Every palette then tints those meshes, so "Prism Crown" and "Ember Circlet" share a shape in different colours while "Prism Crown" and "Geode Beret" are different shapes. Names are individual to each piece, not one palette word repeated down the list.

1. Download a simple SVG icon from an icon library. SVG Repo and The SVG are good starting points.

2. Add a button and select exactly one keyboard key.

3. Import the normal SVG. By default it is recolored to pure black (#000000).

4. A pressed SVG is optional. If you do not provide one, the normal SVG is reused. By default the pressed icon is recolored to #E6E6E6 and shifted down slightly like a Minecraft button.

5. Keep Original Colors lets you preserve the SVG colors separately for normal and pressed states.

6. Icon Size and Icon X/Y Offset adjust the artwork inside the Minecraft-style button. Button Size changes the whole on-screen control.

7. Choose whether the keyboard mapping is momentary or toggle. Momentary holds the mapped key only while you hold the button; toggle alternates key down and key up on each tap.

More Buttons intentionally supports only one key per button and does not provide macros, key sequences, automatic repeats or autoclicking.
